params.question: Which of the following is an absolute indication for caesarean section where vaginal delivery would be impossible or catastrophically dangerous?

answers.text: Failure to progress in active labour despite adequate contractions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Failure to progress is a relative indication — trial of oxytocin augmentation or instrumental delivery may still be attempted before resorting to caesarean section.

answers.text: Major-degree placenta praevia completely covering the internal os

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Major-degree placenta praevia (type III/IV) physically obstructs the birth canal, making vaginal delivery impossible and risking catastrophic maternal haemorrhage. It is a textbook absolute indication.

answers.text: Previous one lower-segment caesarean section with a well-healed scar

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A previous one LSCS is a relative indication. Trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC) is a valid option in selected patients with a well-healed lower-segment scar.
Fetal macrosomia is a relative indication. Many macrosomic infants are delivered vaginally; the decision depends on maternal pelvic capacity, diabetes status, and other clinical factors.

overallFeedback.feedback: Major-degree placenta praevia (type III or IV) is an absolute indication for CS. The placenta completely or partially covers the internal os, physically blocking the birth canal, making vaginal delivery impossible and catastrophically dangerous.
Correct! Major-degree placenta praevia is an absolute indication because the placenta physically obstructs the birth canal — vaginal delivery would risk life-threatening haemorrhage.

params.question: A gynaecologist plans a laparotomy for a patient with a large uterine fibroid measuring 22-weeks' size extending above the umbilicus, along with an ovarian mass of uncertain nature. Which incision is most appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While a Pfannenstiel incision provides better cosmesis, it offers limited exposure of the upper abdomen. A 22-week-sized fibroid extending above the umbilicus with an ovarian mass of uncertain nature demands wider access than a low transverse incision can provide.

answers.text: Low transverse mini-laparotomy to minimise tissue trauma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A mini-laparotomy is suited for small, well-characterised pathology. It would be grossly inadequate for a large fibroid combined with an ovarian mass requiring full abdominal exploration and possible staging.

answers.text: Midline vertical incision for access to both the pelvis and upper abdomen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A midline vertical incision is chosen when the pathology is large (extending above the umbilicus), when upper-abdominal access may be needed, or when the nature of the mass is uncertain — all three criteria apply here.

answers.text: Gridiron incision in the right iliac fossa to target the ovarian pathology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A Gridiron incision is used for appendicectomy, not gynaecological laparotomy. It provides no access to the uterus or contralateral adnexa and would be entirely inappropriate here.

overallFeedback.feedback: A midline vertical incision is indicated when the pathology is large, the nature of the mass is uncertain, or upper-abdominal access may be needed. A Pfannenstiel incision, while cosmetically superior, cannot provide adequate exposure in this scenario.
Correct! A midline vertical incision provides the wide exposure needed for large pelvic masses, upper-abdominal exploration, and pathology of uncertain nature.

interactions.label: During a repeat caesarean section on a patient with two previous lower-segment s

params.question: During a repeat caesarean section on a patient with two previous lower-segment scars, you observe the surgeon markedly slow down after opening the rectus sheath — she palpates gently and uses small scissor bites rather than sweeping cuts. Which surgical step is she performing, and why does it require this caution?

answers.text: Division of the rectus muscles — risk of inferior epigastric vessel injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The rectus muscles are separated in the midline rather than divided, and the surgeon would not need gentle palpation at this step. The inferior epigastric vessels run laterally and are at risk mainly with excessive lateral extension of the Pfannenstiel incision.

answers.text: Opening the parietal peritoneum — risk of bowel adhesions to the anterior wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While bowel adhesions to the anterior abdominal wall can occur after previous surgery, the scenario describes careful dissection in the uterovesical space between the sheath and the lower uterine segment — characteristic of bladder flap mobilisation, not peritoneal entry.

answers.text: Bladder flap dissection — risk of bladder injury from dense adhesions after previous surgery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In women with previous caesarean scars, the bladder often becomes densely adherent to the lower uterine segment. Hurried sharp dissection at this step causes the majority of bladder injuries at CS. Experienced surgeons deliberately slow down, palpate gently, and use small scissor bites.

answers.text: Uterine incision — risk of cutting into an anteriorly situated placenta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An anterior placenta would be managed by ultrasound-guided incision placement, not by the gentle palpation and small scissor bites described. The careful technique in this scenario is characteristic of bladder flap dissection in a scarred uterovesical space.

overallFeedback.feedback: The bladder flap dissection — not the skin incision — is the highest-risk moment in repeat caesarean sections. Dense adhesions from previous surgery make the bladder adherent to the lower uterine segment, and hurried sharp dissection here causes the majority of bladder injuries at CS.

Correct! The bladder flap is the most dangerous moment in repeat LSCS — dense adhesions from previous surgery make the bladder vulnerable, and experienced surgeons deliberately slow down and use gentle technique here.
